newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Convergence connoisseurs eye short end.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Convergence connoisseurs eye short end.

text.p: European long-dated bond convergence is showing signs of exhaustion but the short end of the market still offers exciting yield pick-up plays, analysts said on Thursday.

"At the long ends you can't really go down much," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London. "While fundamentals are not negative we wouldn't recommend people bet on further convergence."

At a time when Italian 10-year yields are close to 80 basis points away from Bunds, Spanish debt is around 60 and Ecu paper is less than 30, analysts could see little to encourage another rush of convergence, especially as European markets are going into their summer lull.
But at the short end, investors can find yield differentials of more than 200 basis points between two-year Italian and German paper.
"Really convergence should move from the long end to the front end, where spreads are still very significant, but that is currently clashing with domestic needs," Giordano said.
For instance, he noted markets were trying to push short rates downward in Spain but the Bank of Spain would have to take into account a relatively strong economy.
Reiner Back, head of fixed income research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in Frankfurt, agreed that the focus was shifting down the curve.
"There is not much left in terms of convergence plays so those remaining convergence plays get more attention, which is why you see so much attention at the short end of the Italian curve," he said.
Two-year Italian paper currently yields 210 basis points more than German notes. The Spanish/German gap is 130 basis points.
As a means of buying into the euro single currency and holding an investment that would give higher yields than Bunds, this strategy lacks in that the debt has only a brief post-EMU lifespan.

But Giordano said investors could profit from the play if EMU continues to look like a likely prospect because short-end yield convergence should accelerate closer to the planned January 1, 1999 euro launch date.
Even the idea of further EMU-oriented political rows does not trouble the long end at the moment, so deconvergence plays are also not recommended.
"The risks of deconvergence are quite low. The argument has been that Bunds are basically a free put on EMU," said Back of Dresdner Kleinwort. "The market is convinced that EMU will start on time."

The only things he could identify that could lead to some spread backtracking would be a surprisingly large rise in German unemployment, unexpected tax shortfalls in France or the possibility of a fresh political crisis in Italy. But all three he said were unlikely to derail EMU or lead to a spread blowout.
Giordano echoed that view, saying, "We find it hard to see events that could lead to a retracement."
Some analysts, such as Bear Stearns chief economist David Brown in London, still see risks further out for EMU bulls.
But Brown said for now there was little to disabuse markets from expectations of a broad EMU launch. "It's the lamp in the window for the markets at the moment."

He argued, however, EMU bulls could be tripped up later due to external market forces, such as a dollar retracement, or a slump in the U.S. or German bond markets, either of which would put pressure on bond markets in general.
